activities.name: monBreezeCompare

config.prompt: The same circulation at two scales — drag the divider:

before.label: the sea breeze
before.text: Land heats faster than water by day, air rises over the land, and cool sea air flows in to replace it; at night it reverses. A circulation you can feel on any beach, on any afternoon.

after.label: the monsoon
after.text: The same physics run at continental scale and seasonal length: a wind system that reverses with the sun, dragging ocean moisture onto land for a wet summer and letting it drain away in a dry winter.

config.why: The Asian summer monsoon is the planet's largest weather system — fresh water for roughly half of humanity, and whole economies scheduled around it.

config.why: Two Indian districts, forty years apart in water, separated by relief: the airmass is wrung out rising over the hills, and the rain shadow takes whatever is left.

config.why: The contemporary strategy layers old and new: revive the recharge structures, harvest the rooftops, meter the pumps — because water, not land, is the monsoon world's scarcest resource.

activities.anchor: The storage strategies above exist because
activities.caption: bet before you read on — what the pump actually lifts
activities.name: monFossilPredict

config.q: In India's north-western breadbasket the water table falls tens of centimetres a year. What is being pumped?
choices: Last year's monsoon, refilled every season
Fossil water — the stored monsoons of past decades
config.why: The bank-account picture fails: pumped faster than recharge replaces it, the groundwater is fossil water in practice — mined today from monsoons that fell decades ago.

activities.name: monItczCompare

config.prompt: The ITCZ's position writes the climate — drag the divider:

before.label: equatorial
before.text: Where the ITCZ sits overhead or nearby most of the year — the Amazon, Congo, Indonesia: hot every month, heavy rain most afternoons by convection, no real seasons.

after.label: tropical continental (savanna)
after.text: Where it passes only in the high-sun season — Nairobi, Darwin, the Sahel: one wet season, one long dry one, grassland and drought-adapted trees.

config.why: The subsiding limb of the Hadley cell creates the great deserts at the same latitudes the rising ITCZ drenches — the calendar of rain, not just its total, decides garden, grassland or desert margin.

activities.anchor: Hazard reduction is not a physics problem
activities.caption: call the magnitude — the deadliest cyclone on record
activities.name: monBholaEstimate

config.prompt: The 1970 Bhola cyclone struck the Bay of Bengal's delta. Roughly how many people died?
config.why: Some 300,000–500,000 — the deadliest tropical cyclone ever recorded. The same coast, better armed with shelters, embankments, warnings and volunteers, now survives comparable storms with dozens of deaths.
config.context: Built deliberately over fifty years: the same coastline and the same storms, a different outcome.

activities.anchor: That is why Bangladesh's shelters and warnings
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the cyclone briefing
activities.name: monCycloneSpot

config.prompt: One line of this cyclone briefing is wrong — click it:
lines: A tropical cyclone forms where sea surface temperatures exceed about 26.5 °C, at least roughly 5° from the equator, with low wind shear.
The Saffir-Simpson categories 1 to 5 measure wind speed.
The deadliest element of a landfalling cyclone is usually the wind itself.
Storm surge can shove the sea 6–10 m ashore in the Bay of Bengal's shallow, funnel-shaped delta.
Hurricane, typhoon and cyclone are one storm, named by ocean.
config.correction: The deadliest element is usually the storm surge — the sea itself shoved ashore; the Bhola toll was overwhelmingly a drowning event.
config.why: Warm ocean air rises, condenses and releases latent heat in a self-feeding engine with a calm eye and a violent eyewall — but the casualty list is written by the water, not the wind.
